2. The facts giving rise to these questions are that there was a suit for declaration of an easement right over the passing of water through a drain "between the respondents and appellants. The suit was decreed on compromise between the parties concerned on 26th March, 1964. The decree-holder-respondents instituted an Execution case which was dismissed for default on 26th June, 1965. The decree-holder-respondents thereafter filed an application before the Munsif who passed the decree for amendment of the decree under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The amendment sought for was the substitution of the word "uttor parsha" appearing in the second line of paragraph 2 of the compromise petition for the words "uttor purba" on the ground that it was a bonafide mistake. It was stated that the decree would be in executable and meaningless unless the amendment was allowed. This application was filed on 6th April, 1966 and was rejected by the Court on 11th May, 1967. This order of rejection was challenged before the High Court in its revisional jurisdiction but the Rule was discharged on final hearing on 25th June, 1970. The decree holders-respondents, thereafter, filed a second Execution case on 10th November, 1970 which was resisted by the judgment-debtor-appellants under section 47 of the Code, on the ground that it was barred by Limitation having not been filed within three years from the date of the dismissal of the 1st Execution case under Article 182 of the Limitation Act. This objection was negatived by the Executing Court, the Lower Appellate Court and the High Court Division in the Second Miscellaneous Appeal. 

 The High Court Division dismissed the appeal holding the decree holder is entitled to the benefit of the provisions of section 14 of the Limitation Act, and as such the second Execution case was not barred by limitation. 

 5. Of this sub-section (2) the only words which need interpretation to resolve the question are "same relief" in the background of the application filed under section 151 of the Code by the decree-holder-respondents which was rejected both by the trial Court and the High Court Division. The relief sought in the application under section 151 of the Code was for the substitution of the words "uttor Parsha" in place of word "uttor purba" occurring in the compromise petition. In that application it was maintained that the decree without the substituted words was meaningless and in executable. The relief that was being sought in the Executing Court was for execution of the decree whereas, under Section 151 the relief sought was for substitution of the words in the com-promise petition instead of the words there, in other words an amendment of the decree The question is whether these two reliefs come within the meaning of the expression "same relief" as occurring in section 14(2) of the Limitation Act Mr. Salam has made references to some decisions of the Indian Jurisdiction to show that the reliefs in the Act, should be of similar nature. The decisions are reported in AIR 1935 Allahabad 323, AIR 1918 Lahore 117, AIR 1935 P.C. 85, AIR 1945 Madras 86, AIR 1948 Bombay 185. The general trend of the Indian High Courts in these decisions as cited shows that the relief concerned must be of similar nature. The view appears to be that the words "same relief" could not be construed so as to look not to the primary relief sought in a proceeding but the ultimate object with which the relief was sought. In the Privy Council case a preliminary mortgage decree was obtained which was amended in some respects not material to be particularised. There were a number of mortgagors interested in the mortgage some of whom preferred an appeal before the High Court against the preliminary decree. On the failure of the appeal before the High Court, the decree-holder sought execution under the preliminary decree. In this background their Lordships of the Privy Council were of the opinion that the application to obtain execution under the preliminary decree was not an application for the same relief as the application to the Court for a final mortgage decree for sale in the suit. The Privy Council did not elaborate the reasons for their decision. What appears, however, as embodied in the decision is that the words "same relief" occurring under section 14(2) cannot but be relief of a similar nature. We do not find anything to depart from this view. 

 6. In the present appeal we find it difficult to bring the prayer for amendment of the decree under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure as the same relief for execution of unammended decree, within meaning of expression same relief" occurring in section 14(2) of the Limitation Act. 

 In this view, the appeal is allowed but in the facts of case we make no order as to costs. The decrees of courts below are set aside and the execution petition dismissed.
